title: The p-value on the experience-advantage comparison reproduces under no test
published: This difference is not statistically significant (p = [[0.791]]).
corrected: This difference is not statistically significant (p = [[0.852]]).
note: The corrected figure is a regression of the more-experienced-candidate-wins indicator on ballot type with HC2 standard errors. A chi-squared test of the same two-by-two table gives 0.919, and no standard test of this comparison returns 0.791. The conclusion the sentence draws is unaffected: the difference of 0.8 percentage points is not distinguishable from zero on any of them. No other sentence quotes the p-value, so "not statistically significant" is the whole of what it holds up.

title: The number of municipalities in the mayoral election dataset
location: p. 576, Information Shortcuts in Nonpartisan Elections
published: This dataset covers [[225]] unique municipalities and records background characteristics of winners and runners-up, contextual information such as electoral rules, and electoral outcomes.
corrected: This dataset covers [[237]] unique municipalities and records background characteristics of winners and runners-up, contextual information such as electoral rules, and electoral outcomes.
note: The file carries 237 distinct FIPS place codes across its 1010 elections, and it is the file the sentence describes: the election count and the 1945 to 2007 span both reproduce exactly. No other reading of it returns 225 either, since municipalities holding more than one election number 171, the subset used later in the paragraph covers 216, and truncating the place code to five digits gives 213. No quantity in the article is computed over municipalities: Table 1 and the experience-advantage comparison count elections, so the correction changes the description of the dataset and nothing derived from it.

title: The range of political experience effects is stated more tightly than the estimates support
published: Relative to a candidate with no political experience, respondents prefer candidates who are City Council Members, State Legislators, Mayors, or Representatives in Congress by a margin of [[25--30]] percentage points.
corrected: Relative to a candidate with no political experience, respondents prefer candidates who are City Council Members, State Legislators, Mayors, or Representatives in Congress by a margin of [[23--32]] percentage points.
note: The published range is wrong at both ends rather than at one. The four estimates in the nonpartisan column of Figure 3 are Representative in Congress 25.2, Mayor 32.0, State Legislator 25.3, City Council Member 22.7 percentage points. The claim the sentence makes is unaffected: political experience remains by a wide margin the most consequential attribute in the figure, and the next largest effect of any kind is 5.5 percentage points. The corrected upper end also bears on the sentence that follows, that candidates who had been mayor "were rewarded most": Mayor's 32.0 stands 6.7 points above the next largest, State Legislator's 25.3, a lead the published range understated.

title: The racial preference pattern holds in one sample and not the other
published: Republican respondents marginally prefer white candidates while Democrats marginally prefer nonwhite candidates.
corrected: Republican respondents marginally prefer white candidates [[in the YouGov sample]], while Democrats marginally prefer nonwhite [[candidates in both]].
note: The Democratic half of the sentence holds everywhere: all six estimates are positive, Asian +4.0, Black +6.1, Hispanic +1.5 percentage points on Mechanical Turk and Asian +3.0, Black +9.1, Hispanic +0.0 on YouGov, the last of those being +0.018 rather than a true zero. The Republican half holds only on YouGov, where the three estimates are Asian -5.9, Black -6.7, Hispanic -9.3. On Mechanical Turk, Republican respondents prefer **Asian** candidates to white candidates by 6.1 percentage points, while preferring white candidates to Black ones by 9.8 and to Hispanic ones by 4.3. A reader taking the sentence as a general finding about Republican respondents would be taking a pattern that reverses on one of the paper's two samples. The qualification applies under both ballots, which keeps the next sentence's "these race and gender patterns do not differ much by election type" true: in partisan elections the Republican estimates are Asian +0.1, Black +1.3, Hispanic -4.1 on Mechanical Turk and Asian -8.2, Black -13.0, Hispanic -10.5 on YouGov. Nothing later in the article rests on the race pattern, which it offers as one of "some small patterns"; the abstract and the Discussion rest on political and career experience.

title: Republican respondents do show a competence gap by election type
published: As shown in the difference column, Democratic respondents ([[but not Republican respondents]]) rate such candidates as even more competent in the absence of party labels.
corrected: As shown in the difference column, Democratic respondents ([[and, for candidates who have been mayor, Republican respondents]]) rate such candidates as even more competent in the absence of party labels.
note: The parenthetical reads the Republican half of Figure 7's difference column as null, and one of its four estimates is not. 2 of the 4 Democratic intervals exclude zero and so does 1 of the 4 Republican ones: Republican respondents rate a candidate who has been mayor 4.74 points more competent in nonpartisan than in partisan elections, with a 95 per cent interval of 0.23 to 9.25. The contrast the sentence draws is one of degree rather than of presence. What the parenthetical held up is the section's parallel between the two outcomes: "the same candidate types that respondents view as more competent are the ones that they tend to elect at higher rates in nonpartisan elections." For Democratic respondents the parallel holds. For the corrected Republican cell it does not, since in Figure 5's difference column the same respondents are 3.3 percentage points less likely to choose a former mayor in nonpartisan elections (95 per cent interval -13.7 to 7.0). It is also one Republican interval in 9: Figure 8's YouGov difference column has 0 of 5 Republican intervals excluding zero (and 3 of 5 Democratic ones), and at the 5 per cent level chance alone gives 0.45 such intervals in 9. The competence argument survives, resting on Democratic respondents, who are also the ones for whom the vote-choice results bear out the paper's main prediction.

title: The two ballot types are transposed in the experience-advantage comparison
published: Subsetting our dataset to only those elections in which candidates have different levels of political experience (779 elections), we see that the candidate with more experience wins about [[62%]] of the time in [[partisan]] elections and [[61%]] of the time in [[nonpartisan]] elections.
corrected: Subsetting our dataset to only those elections in which candidates have different levels of political experience (779 elections), we see that the candidate with more experience wins about [[62%]] of the time in [[nonpartisan]] elections and [[61%]] of the time in [[partisan]] elections.
note: Both percentages are right and the labels attached to them are the wrong way round. The data give 62.1 per cent in nonpartisan elections and 61.3 per cent in partisan elections, across the 779 elections the sentence identifies. The direction matters here, because the article's own argument is that nonpartisan ballots favour the more experienced candidate: the published sentence reports the gap running the other way. What the sentence holds up is the paragraph's verdict that this analysis "paints a murkier picture". Corrected, the gap runs the way the paper predicts, by 0.8 percentage points at p = 0.852 (entry 1), so the verdict survives on the absence of a difference rather than on its sign. The observational support the Discussion draws on is Table 1, which this entry does not touch.

title: Oliver, Ha and Callen (2012) is missing its third author
published: [[Oliver, J. E., & Ha, S. E.]] (2012). Local Elections and the Politics of Small-Scale Democracy. Princeton: Princeton University Press.
corrected: Oliver, J. E., Ha, S. E., & Callen, Z. (2012). Local Elections and the Politics of Small-Scale Democracy. Princeton: Princeton University Press.
note: The book has three authors. Crossref, doi 10.23943/princeton/9780691143552.001.0001: Oliver, J. Eric; Ha, Shang E.; Callen, Zachary. The article's own in-text citation on p. 588 reads "Oliver et al. 2012", which the two-author entry cannot support. No claim in the article rests on the author list; what the correction restores is the reference's function, that the citation leads a reader to the book it names.
